title: Flexible reservation & SLA triage playbook: recommended GPU class, burst lanes, and preemption rules
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: Sales and Customer Success regularly submit enterprise dedicated capacity requests with inconsistent intake data (desired RPS/latency, target SLOs, model family, prompt length distribution, peak burst characteristics). Current triage is ad-hoc and often leads to oversized or undersized reservations, SLA misses, and manual follow-ups.

Goal: Produce an operational playbook and deterministic scoring algorithm to intake, prioritize, and recommend: target SLA (p50/p95 latency), reserved throughput (tokens/sec or RPS), GPU class (A100/RTX-8k/Hopper-equivalents), and scaling policy (slow/fast autoscale, warm pool size, preemption exemptions). The playbook should be prescriptive enough to return a recommended configuration to Sales within 48 hours for ~80% of requests and provide a clear path for exceptions that require deeper perf validation.
acceptance_criteria: A documented intake form that collects latency target, qps/tokens, prompt/response length distribution, model family, tolerance for 5xx/backoff, expected peak burst duration and frequency.
A triage rubric with numeric weights for SLA criticality, customer business impact, model compute intensity, burstiness, and compliance constraints.
A deterministic mapping from requested throughput and model footprint to a recommended GPU class and a min/max GPU count estimate (with assumptions stated).
Recommendation engine returns a prescriptive staging config (reserved GPUs, warm pool, preemption policy) within 48 hours for typical requests.
Runbook for 'exception' cases that require perf validation (benchmarks, KV cache warmup tests) including checklist and owner assignment.
Stakeholders (sales/solutions/infra/eng) sign-off on playbook and rollout plan.
proposed_solution: 1) Standardize an intake questionnaire and make it mandatory for any reserved capacity request. 2) Implement a 5-factor scoring rubric (SLA criticality 30%, throughput 25%, model compute intensity 20%, burstiness 15%, compliance constraints 10%). 3) Codify GPU recommendation rules: map model family + avg seq len + tokens/sec to a GPU class baseline and provide a conservative buffer factor (x1.25 for unknowns). 4) Define three reserved profiles: 'Steady', 'Burst-capable', 'Mission-critical' — each with default warm-pool %, autoscale ramp rates, and preemption exceptions. 5) Publish templates for Sales to present recommended configs and cost/latency trade-offs. 6) Add a lightweight internal service (CSV + rule engine) to produce the initial recommendation; handoffs for exception cases to Performance Engineering with explicit benchmarks.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (2 weeks): finalize intake form and scoring rubric; socialization with Solutions and Sales; align on label taxonomy. Phase 2 (4 weeks): implement recommendation rules in a lightweight spreadsheet/tool, pilot with 6 incoming requests, collect feedback. Phase 3 (2 weeks): automate recommendation generation (internal UI or API), add expected cost delta estimates, and train Sales. Phase 4 (ongoing): refine mapping using telemetry from runtime (tokens/sec, p95 latency) and closed-loop adjustments. Post-launch: run monthly calibration sessions with Perf Eng to update GPU mapping and buffer factors.
metrics: Fraction of requests answered without engineering benching >= 80%
Percentage of reservations that meet p95 SLA in first 14 days >= 90%
Average overprovision buffer (cost delta) across pilots, target < 25%
Number of exception escalations per month (target <= 3)
risks: Mapping rules may under/over-provision for novel model families (risk mitigated by buffer factor and exception path).
Sales bypassing intake form causing incomplete data — requires enforcement and playbook adoption.
GPU availability constraints in cloud regions could force inferior GPU classes; need coupling with capacity planning (Dedicated team).
Automated recommendations could be misinterpreted as guarantees — messaging and templated disclaimers required.
